name: Financial Times cryptic crossword No 13,893
preamble: Each across clue is broadly thematic and may not include a thematic definition of the solution.

solutions.check: grid and clues read from the FT's printable PDF, its numbering matching the clue list; every fifteensquared answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

indicators.note: most of something is all but a part of it, so the word loses its final letter
one who eats takes food inside, so the first word swallows the second

blocks.note: Kate is the title shrew in Shakespeare's The Taming of the Shrew
a rat is a rodent; cut short it gives RA

explanation.surface: A shrew devouring nearly all of a larger rodent: a gruesome bit of nature footage.
explanation.walkthrough: The preamble says across clues may lack a definition; this one has none, and the answer is simply a sport.
explanation.definitionFit: The across entries are all games and sports, and this martial art fought barehanded is one of them.

indicators.note: demolishing knocks a thing down to rubble, so its letters are broken up and rebuilt

blocks.note: the letters of teak rearranged
Dubya is the nickname of US president George W. Bush

explanation.surface: A singer and George W. Bush together smashing up teak furniture.
explanation.definitionFit: She is the English singer-songwriter of Wuthering Heights, a pop star since the late 1970s.

blocks.note: a runner is someone who has fled
to be up is to be brought before a court

explanation.surface: An escaped prisoner turns up in court for the second time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Second' looks like an ordinal number in the surface; here it means the one who comes second.
explanation.definitionFit: The competitor who finishes second, just behind the winner, is given this title.

clue.text: Least clever rustic in international match

indicators.note: in places one word inside the other

blocks.note: a Test is an international cricket or rugby match
a hick is an unsophisticated country person

explanation.surface: The dimmest country bumpkin turns out for an international game.
explanation.definitionFit: Thick means stupid, so the superlative describes the most stupid one.

indicators.note: something wrong is out of order, so these letters need rearranging

blocks.note: la is the French feminine word for the
the letters of score's, apostrophe dropped, rearranged

explanation.surface: A complaint that a French scoreline has been reported wrongly.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's of score's is part of the anagram fodder, not a link to the indicator.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the field game played with a netted stick, one of the sports the across entries share.

indicators.note: upset means knocked over and disordered, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: posh means first-rate, A1, written with the letter I for the digit
the letters of garb rearranged

explanation.surface: Smart clothes knocked about by a car's safety feature.
explanation.walkthrough: A1 meaning top-class is often written AI in crosswords.
explanation.definitionFit: This cushion inflates in a crash to protect a car's occupants, a safety device.

blocks.note: first meaning: an eraser for pencil marks
second meaning: a match of games in the card game at 27 across

explanation.walkthrough: 27 across is the card game whose matches are scored as best of three games.
explanation.definitionFit: The British word for an eraser is also the term for a set of games in bridge.

blocks.note: a seam is a join between two pieces
an means one, the indefinite article

explanation.surface: An order to enlist one more sailor.
explanation.definitionFit: A seaman is a sailor, especially one below officer rank.

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter is kept

blocks.note: Eve is a girl's name
the first, third and fifth letters

explanation.surface: A girl called Nelly who does something regularly, with emphasis.
explanation.walkthrough: The first 'regularly' picks alternate letters; the repeat with an exclamation mark is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something evenly means at a steady, uniform rate, which is what regularly also means.

clue.text: First service – and where not to put it, on reflection

indicators.note: first asks for only the opening letter of the following word
a reflection in a mirror shows things the other way round, so the whole string is read backwards

blocks.note: the opening letter of service
a serve that goes in the net is a fault, so that is where not to put it

explanation.surface: Advice on serving: get the first serve in, and keep it out of the net.
explanation.walkthrough: The string S + IN NET is read backwards. The whole clue also describes the game, so the missing definition is hardly missed.
explanation.definitionFit: The racket game with serves and a net is one of the sports that make up the across entries.

indicators.note: tossed things are thrown about and land jumbled, so the letters are mixed up

blocks.note: the fodder, taken letter by letter

explanation.surface: A Highland games competitor has thrown a huge caber.
explanation.walkthrough: Tossing the caber is a real Scottish event, so 'Tossed' reads naturally as the surface verb; a caber is a tree trunk.
explanation.definitionFit: This card game scored with pegs on a board is one of the games shared by the across entries.

blocks.note: first meaning: runs of points made in one visit to the table
second meaning: school intervals between classes

explanation.surface: A schoolboy plays snooker in the gaps between his classes.
explanation.walkthrough: Snooker is a cue game; a player's continuous scoring run is so called.
explanation.definitionFit: The same plural noun names a snooker player's scoring sequences and the rest periods in a school timetable.

blocks.note: base means lowly, of inferior class
a ball is a formal dance

explanation.surface: A dance held for the lower orders, as a snob might call it.
explanation.definitionFit: This American bat-and-ball game is one of the sports that make up the across entries.

clue.text: Gives away young girl to boy on Sunday

blocks.note: Bet is a pet form of Elizabeth
Ray is a boy's name
S is the abbreviation for Sunday

explanation.surface: A father gives his daughter away to her groom at a Sunday wedding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gives away' suggests a bride; it means reveals or is disloyal to.
explanation.definitionFit: To betray someone is to give them away to an enemy, or to give away a secret.

blocks.note: a leg is a limb, a member of the body
bye is a word of farewell

explanation.surface: A spare limb saying goodbye, or an extra performer making an exit.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket, an extra is a run not credited to the batsman; this one is scored after the ball hits the batsman's body.
explanation.definitionFit: In cricket this run off the batsman's body counts among the extras, not the batsman's own score.

blocks.note: the letter written before the hyphen, taken as it stands
to quash is to crush or suppress

explanation.surface: A playful question: is it crush, or a stammered s-crush?
explanation.walkthrough: The hyphen splits off S, and 'crush' is then read as a synonym, so 'Crush or s-crush' is the answer twice over. The answer is also the racket sport.
explanation.definitionFit: To squeeze something flat is to flatten or squash it, a plain synonym for the verb.

indicators.note: some means a part of, so the answer is a run of letters inside the next word

blocks.note: letters two to four of this word

explanation.surface: A snapshot that was lifted only lately.
explanation.definitionFit: Hot is slang for stolen goods still being searched for, freshly stolen and risky to handle.

indicators.note: upset means turned upside down, which in a down entry reverses the letters

blocks.note: per means for each, as in per person

explanation.surface: An agent who gets annoyed at every turn.
explanation.definitionFit: A rep, short for representative, is a sales agent acting for a firm.

clue.text: Desire about trip before US sports event

indicators.note: about can mean turned round, so the word for desire is read backwards

blocks.note: a tour is a trip
a yen is a longing or desire; read backwards it goes after the trip

explanation.surface: Someone longing to travel to America for a big sporting fixture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'before' places the trip ahead of the turned-round desire.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is a chiefly American informal term for a tournament, a sporting competition.

clue.text: Such times of yore – saga translated

indicators.note: translated means turned into a different form, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the fodder, taken letter by letter

explanation.surface: An old Norse saga, rendered into another language, tells of times long past.
explanation.walkthrough: The fodder is itself about the distant past, so the surface nearly defines the answer twice.
explanation.definitionFit: Times of yore are times long past, which is what the phrase meaning long ago describes.

blocks.note: first meaning: to be reluctant to act
second meaning: to restrain or restrict

explanation.walkthrough: Two verbs joined by 'and', each a meaning of the same phrasal verb.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb means both to refrain from acting and to restrain something or someone.

clue.text: Drake swimming into inlet in time for teacher training

indicators.note: swimming things move about freely, so the letters are mixed up
into places the shuffled letters inside the word for inlet

blocks.note: the letters of Drake rearranged
a bay is an inlet of the sea

explanation.surface: A male duck paddles into a creek just in time for a training session.
explanation.walkthrough: A baker day is a UK school closure day for staff training, named after Kenneth Baker, the education secretary who introduced them.
explanation.definitionFit: These school days, when pupils stay home, were set aside by Kenneth Baker for in-service teacher training.

clue.text: Amateur taking exercise by patch of ground first

indicators.note: first places the earlier-named items ahead of the amateur in the final order

blocks.note: PE is physical education, exercise at school
a lot is a plot or patch of land
A is the abbreviation for amateur

explanation.surface: An amateur athlete exercising on a small plot before anything else.
explanation.definitionFit: This Basque court game played with a wicker basket against a wall is one of the sports among the across entries.

indicators.note: capricious means changeable and unpredictable, so the letters change places

blocks.note: the fodder; oreads are mountain nymphs

explanation.surface: Fickle mountain nymphs being worshipped, or doing the worshipping.
explanation.definitionFit: To adore is to revere or worship, so the third-person form matches the verb.

blocks.note: I is the Roman numeral for one
an MP is a Member of Parliament
the Ure is a river in Yorkshire

explanation.surface: A rude remark by one unmarried MP while on the river.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry, 'on' puts the earlier pieces above the river.
explanation.definitionFit: Impure thoughts are unchaste ones, so the adjective serves as a synonym for lewd.

blocks.note: in means fashionable, popular
a deed is an act

explanation.surface: A performance that is extremely well liked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Very' looks like an intensifier for popular; it is the definition, as in 'very well, indeed'.
explanation.definitionFit: Indeed works as an emphatic adverb after an adjective, just as very works before one.

indicators.note: round suggests the letters are turned about and rearranged

blocks.note: the fodder, taken letter by letter

explanation.surface: A large woman standing a round of drinks at the pub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Big Bertha' is a set phrase, first the German heavy gun of the First World War, hence the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Big Bertha is the familiar name for anything outsized, so this girl's name follows big naturally.

blocks.note: first meaning, as the setter has it: errors, blunders
second meaning: half-masks worn with a hooded cloak at masquerades

explanation.walkthrough: The masks sense is the standard one, a domino being a masquerade mask; dictionaries do not commonly list the mistakes sense, so that half is the setter's stretch. The game itself is not defined, as the preamble allows.
explanation.definitionFit: A domino is a small eye-mask or masquerade cloak, so the plural names a set of masks.

clue.text: It's not pontoon – or is it?

definitions.text: It's not pontoon – or is it?

blocks.note: surface reading: pontoon is a card game, so this is some other card game
setter's reading: a pontoon is also a floating span over water, so it may be this after all

explanation.walkthrough: Pontoon is the British name for the card game blackjack, but a pontoon is also a floating crossing, which is the second, structural meaning of this card game's name.
explanation.definitionFit: The partnership card game is not pontoon, yet a pontoon is a kind of crossing over a river, which the same word names.

indicators.note: something happening during an event falls within it, so one word sits inside the other

blocks.note: a route is the way of a journey
to let is to allow, to give the OK

explanation.surface: Someone approving a plan while already on the road.
explanation.definitionFit: The casino game with a spinning wheel and ball is one of the games that make up the across entries.

clue.text: Difficulty is severe, round centre of maze

indicators.note: the centre of a word is its middle, so only the middle letters are kept
one thing round another encloses it, so the word for severe wraps the kept letters

blocks.note: the two middle letters of maze
hard means harsh or severe

explanation.surface: Getting lost in a maze can be a severe problem.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is also an old dice game, the thematic sense the preamble lets go undefined.
explanation.definitionFit: A hazard is a danger or obstacle, so it serves as a synonym for a difficulty.

blocks.note: speed is slang for amphetamine
will and way both mean what one wants, as in having one's way

explanation.surface: A legal note about drugs left in a will, or a declaration that amphetamine will do it.
explanation.definitionFit: This motorcycle racing on an oval dirt track is one of the sports shared by the across entries.

clue.text: Nameless artist having wine early, outside

indicators.note: nameless means without N, the abbreviation for name, so that letter is removed

blocks.note: David Hockney, the English painter
surface padding here, though it also spells the letters a second way, as the walkthrough says

explanation.surface: A painter with no name drinking wine early in the day out of doors.
explanation.walkthrough: The rest of the clue gives the same letters a second way: HOCK, a German white wine, then EY, the outside letters of early.
explanation.definitionFit: This stick-and-ball game, on ice or on a field, is one of the sports that make up the across entries.
